Law governing the culpability of Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 Legislative provisions 9. Section 138 of the NI Act provides as under:-
"138. Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account. - Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for PRANJAL ANEJA ANEJA Date:

4 2025.06.06 15:54:38 +0530 a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both:
Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless- (a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier;
(b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice.
Explanation:- For the purposes of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability."

sentences.text: Relevant Judicial pronouncements 11.

It has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rangappa vs. Sri Mohan, (2010) 11 SCC 441 that :
".... the presumption mandated by Section 139 of the Act does indeed include the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability.

... 
Section 139 of the Act is an example of a reverse onus clause that has been included in furtherance of the legislative objective to improve the credibility of negotiable instruments.

While Section 138 of the Act specifies a strong criminal remedy in relation to the cheques, the rebuttable presumption under Section 139 is a device to prevent undue delay in the course of litigation.

However, it must be remembered that the PRANJAL ANEJA ANEJA 2025.06.06 15:54:53 +0530 offence made punishable by Section 138 can be better described as a regulatory offence since the bouncing of a cheque is largely in the nature of a civil wrong whose impact is usually confined to the private parties involved in commercial transactions.

In such a scenario, the test of proportionality should guide the construction and interpretation of reverse onus clauses and the accused/defendant cannot be expected to discharge an unduly high standard of proof.
In the absence of compelling justifications, reverse onus clauses usually impose an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden.
Keeping this in view, it is a settled position that when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139, the standard of proof for doing so is that of 'preponderance of probabilities'.
Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail.

As clarified in the citations, the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own."

12. It has been held in Hiten P Dalal vs. Bratindranath Banerjee, (2001) 6 SCC 16 that a mere plausible explanation given by the accused is not enough to rebut the presumption and the accused has to necessarily disprove the prosecution case by leading Digitally signed PRANJAL by PRANJAL ANEJA ANEJA

sentences.text: In view of the aforesaid proposition of law laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court, it has to be seen as to whether the respondent/complainant has been able to prove that there was legally enforceable debt or liability for which the cheque in question was issued by the appellant/accused or that the appellant/accused has been able to rebut the presumption and prove that the cheque in question had not been issued in discharge of legally enforceable debt or liability.
The complainant in a case of Section 138 NI Act, in order to succeed, has to satisfy the legal ingredients of this provision viz. (1)

that a person has drawn a cheque, on his bank account for payment of any amount to another person from that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any legally enforceable debt or other liability (2) presentment of that cheque to the bank within time (3) cheque returned by drawee bank unpaid due to insufficient balance or exceeding arrangement (4) payee makes a demand notice in writing to the drawer within 30 days of receipt of information from the bank as to dishonour of the cheque (5) drawer fails to make said payment to payee within 15 days of receipt of that legal notice.

14. As such, once the issuance of the cheque is admitted or proved, the court is duty bound to raise a presumption that the dishonoured cheque placed before it was indeed issued in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability of the amount mentioned therein.

Of course, the said presumption is rebuttable one and it is for the accused to prove that the cheque in question had not been issued in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or PRANJAL ANEJA ANEJA Date:
2025.06.06 15:55:09 +0530 liability.
Analysis and Conclusion 15.

It is a cardinal principle of criminal jurisprudence that it is the burden of the prosecution to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt, however the statutory presumptions wherever are available to the accused create an exception to this cardinal principle by shifting the burden of proof to the opposite party.

Among the notable presumptions available under the scheme of the NI Act, two are available under Sections 118 (a) and 139 of the Act, the contours of which have been cited and discussed in the above mentioned judicial pronouncements.

16. In the instant case, the respondent/complainant filed the original cheque dated 21.03.2017 Ex.CW-1/B, its return memo dated 05.04.2017 Ex. CW-1/C, legal notice dated 24.04.2017 Ex.
CW1/D, its speed post receipt dated 26.04.2017 Ex.CW1/E and postal tracking/service report Ex.CW1/F on record during the trial.

During the trial, in his statement U/s 313 Cr.P.C, accused admitted his signatures on the cheque in question and in his statement u/s 294 Cr.P.C. he also admitted the cheque return memo (with reason 'insufficient funds').
He also admitted the receipt of legal notice.
Admittedly, despite service of the legal notice, there is no payment of the cheque amount by the accused/ appellant.
The cheque in question is dated 21.03.2017 and cheque return memo bears the date as 05.04.2017, therefore, the cheque in question is duly presented within its validity period of three months.
The legal notice dated 24.04.2017 Ex.CW1/D has been sent vide speed post receipt dated 26.04.2017.
Thus, the legal notice is served within the statutory period of 30 days from the date of the cheque return memo.

As per speed post tracking Digitally signed by PRANJAL PRANJAL ANEJA ANEJA Date:

sentences.text: Admittedly, no payment has been made by the appellant/ accused in response to the legal notice.
The present complaint u/s 138 NI Act was filed on 29.05.2017 well within the statutory period of one month from the end of the aforesaid 15 days time given for making payment.
The complaint is therefore within limitation.
17. It is thus seen that out of all the ingredients necessary to convict a person U/s 138 NI Act as discussed in para 14 above, the ingredients from 2 to 5 are satisfied.
The only ingredient which now remains is whether the cheque in question has been issued in discharge, in whole or in part, of any legally enforceable debt or other liability.

18. The appellant/ accused admitted his signatures on the cheque in question, however, in his statement recorded u/s 313 Cr.P.C, he stated that he had given blank cheque to the complainant and other particulars are not filled by him thus implying that he did not fill the particulars.

In this regard, it would be apt to refer to the authority of Bir Singh Vs. Mukesh Kumar (2019) 4 SCC 197,
wherein, it was held by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India that a meaningful reading of the provisions of NI Act including, in particular, Sections 20, 87 and 139, makes it amply clear that a person who signs a cheque and makes it over to the payee remains liable unless he adduces evidence to rebut the presumption that the cheque had been issued for payment of a debt or in discharge of a liability.

It was further held that it is immaterial that the cheque may have been filled in by any person other than the drawer, if the cheque is Digitally signed by PRANJAL PRANJAL ANEJA ANEJA Date:
2025.06.06 15:55:23 +0530 duly signed by the drawer and even a blank cheque leaf,
voluntarily signed and handed over by the accused, which is towards some payment,
would attract presumption U/s 139, in the absence of any cogent evidence to show that the cheque was not issued in discharge of a debt.
Thus, in view of above authority, the defence of the appellant/ accused that he merely gave a blank cheque is of no help to him.
19. The appellant/accused in the present case has admitted his signatures on the cheque in question.

Thus, as per the authority laid down under Rangappa (supra) and Bir Singh (supra), the presumptions of Section 118 (a) and 139 NI Act comes into play and the burden is upon the accused to rebut these presumptions by raising probable defence either by relying upon the material submitted by the complainant or by leading cogent and reliable evidence.

20. The accused/appellant has tried to rebut the presumption by alleging that he has made a down payment of Rs.25,000/- but the same has not been adjusted in the loan amount and also that the vehicle has been sold for Rs.22,000/- which is an undervalued price.
He further contends that he has some liability but not to the extent of the cheque amount.

26. Therefore, I find no illegality or infirmity in the judgment dated 12.10.2022 passed by the Ld.
Trial Court thereby convicting the appellant/accused for the offence punishable under Digitally signed by PRANJAL PRANJAL ANEJA ANEJA Date:

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Law governing the culpability of Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 Legislative provisions 9. Section 138 of the NI Act provides as under:-
"138. Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account. - Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for PRANJAL ANEJA ANEJA Date:
Bharat Singh vs Pooja Finlease Ltd on 6 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/111920284/
4 2025.06.06 15:54:38 +0530 a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both:
Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless- (a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier;
(b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice.
Explanation:- For the purposes of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability."
10.
Alongside, it would also be expedient to refer to the legal presumptions which go hand-in-hand with Section 138 that are laid down under Section 118 (a) and Section 139 of the NI Act reproduced as under:-
Section 118 (a) NI Act reads as under :
"Presumptions as to Negotiable Instruments - Until the contrary is proved, the following presumption shall be made ; -

5 Section 139 NI Act reads as under :
Presumption in favour of holder It shall be presumed, unless contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability.

6 13.
The complainant in a case of Section 138 NI Act, in order to succeed, has to satisfy the legal ingredients of this provision viz. (1)
that a person has drawn a cheque, on his bank account for payment of any amount to another person from that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any legally enforceable debt or other liability (2) presentment of that cheque to the bank within time (3) cheque returned by drawee bank unpaid due to insufficient balance or exceeding arrangement (4) payee makes a demand notice in writing to the drawer within 30 days of receipt of information from the bank as to dishonour of the cheque (5) drawer fails to make said payment to payee within 15 days of receipt of that legal notice.
14. As such, once the issuance of the cheque is admitted or proved, the court is duty bound to raise a presumption that the dishonoured cheque placed before it was indeed issued in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability of the amount mentioned therein.
Of course, the said presumption is rebuttable one and it is for the accused to prove that the cheque in question had not been issued in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or PRANJAL ANEJA ANEJA Date:
2025.06.06 15:55:09 +0530 liability.
It is a cardinal principle of criminal jurisprudence that it is the burden of the prosecution to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt, however the statutory presumptions wherever are available to the accused create an exception to this cardinal principle by shifting the burden of proof to the opposite party.
Admittedly, despite service of the legal notice, there is no payment of the cheque amount by the accused/ appellant.
The cheque in question is dated 21.03.2017 and cheque return memo bears the date as 05.04.2017, therefore, the cheque in question is duly presented within its validity period of three months.
The legal notice dated 24.04.2017 Ex.CW1/D has been sent vide speed post receipt dated 26.04.2017.
Thus, the legal notice is served within the statutory period of 30 days from the date of the cheque return memo.
But Bharat Singh vs Pooja Finlease Ltd on 6 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/111920284/
8
It is rather not acceptable that a person takes loan and at the same time makes some down payment to the same person to be deducted from the loan amount.
Nowhere in his defence, the accused stated any specific amount which he owes to the complainant.
Thus, merely denying the cheque amount and stating that he has 'some liability' is not sufficient to rebut the presumption u/s 139 NI Act standing against him.
Consequently appellant /accused has failed to rebut the presumptions u/s 118(a) and 139 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 standing against him.

10
Thus, in light of the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case and under the light of the submissions as made by both the sides, I do not consider to impose any substantive sentence of imprisonment upon the accused / appellant as the same would serve no purpose, however, I find imposing fine / compensation to the tune of Rs.32,000/- to be just and fair which would meet the ends of justice in this case.
opennyai_summary.issue: In view of the aforesaid proposition of law laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court, it has to be seen as to whether the respondent/complainant has been able to prove that there was legally enforceable debt or liability for which the cheque in question was issued by the appellant/accused or that the appellant/accused has been able to rebut the presumption and prove that the cheque in question had not been issued in discharge of legally enforceable debt or liability.
opennyai_summary.arguments: Thus, as per the authority laid down under Rangappa (supra) and Bir Singh (supra), the presumptions of Section 118 (a) and 139 NI Act comes into play and the burden is upon the accused to rebut these presumptions by raising probable defence either by relying upon the material submitted by the complainant or by leading cogent and reliable evidence.
